builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
summary: HoS replaces finetuning-based prompt injection defenses (e.g., SecAlign++) and architectural separation schemes (e.g., ASIDE) with a small set of learned per-head attention gates that redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens. It requires access to model weights and a training procedure to learn the gates, which is impractical for API-only models and demanding for a 70B model on a single 24 GB GPU, though feasible for a quantized ~20B model; inference overhead appears negligible once gates are trained. It can fail against stronger adaptive attacks not covered in evaluation, and robustness may not transfer if the gating is learned on a narrow attack distribution.
rationale: The defense shows strong robustness gains over finetuning baselines without degrading utility, but adopting it requires model-weight access and a gate-training pipeline, so it warrants small-scale validation on an open ~20B model before production commitment.
technique: Learned per-head attention gates for prompt injection defense

claims.statement: HoS replaces finetuning-based prompt injection defenses (e.g., SecAlign++) and architectural separation schemes (e.g., ASIDE) with a small set of learned per-head attention gates that redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens. It requires access to model weights and a training procedure to learn the gates, which is impractical for API-only models and demanding for a 70B model on a single 24 GB GPU, though feasible for a quantized ~20B model; inference overhead appears negligible once gates are trained. It can fail against stronger adaptive attacks not covered in evaluation, and robustness may not transfer if the gating is learned on a narrow attack distribution.

Under the black-box RL-Hammer attack, attack success rate drops from 85% for SecAlign (97% for the undefended GPT-OSS-20B) to 10% for HoS; the white-box Claudini attack needs 3x more FLOPs to reach the same ASR against HoS as against baselines.
